entries.content: The thing that caught me off guard was how much other drivers pressure you to go faster or take shortcuts. Had someone honking at me for waiting at a yield sign when I wasn't comfortable merging yet. Instructor told me to ignore them and trust my own judgment about what's safe.

Been driving this area for 8 years now. There are certain spots where the posted rules don't match how traffic actually flows. The city knows about it but updating signage costs money and creates liability issues, so they leave old signs up while enforcement focuses elsewhere. I just watch what the regulars do and follow their lead - they know which rules are vestigial.

Noticed the intersection at Oak and 5th has a restriction sign but steady traffic ignoring it throughout the day. Asked a neighbor who's lived here 20 years - she said the sign went up after a construction project years ago and was never removed. Local police apparently told her they don't bother with it anymore since the original reason for the restriction is gone.

Moving violations remain on driving records for 3-5 years depending on state. Insurance companies review records at renewal and may increase premiums by 15-25% per violation. New drivers with violations in their first year often face the steepest rate increases due to limited driving history.

A practical approach is observing traffic patterns over several days at different times. When you see consistent behavior from multiple drivers - especially during peak hours when police presence is higher - that gives you useful information about local norms. Longtime residents often develop an intuitive sense of which posted rules reflect current traffic engineering priorities versus legacy signage that hasn't been updated. Delivery drivers and rideshare operators who drive the same routes daily tend to have reliable instincts about this.
